# Digest slice 7 — Thielman Ephesians §XI (5:15–6:9)

## Coverage
Read lines 1–531 in full (the whole of §XI: 5:15–20 intro + 5:21–6:9 household code, including Exegesis/Exposition, Summaries, and Additional Notes). Lines 533–623 **OVERFLOW** past my scope endpoint (6:9) into §XII "Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)" — the armor of God and pseudonymity discussion. Overflow noted below in a separate section; not extracted in full detail since out of assigned scope. No internal duplication detected (the repeated section-header/outline blocks at lines 1–5, 96–100, 533–539 are Thielman's running TOC banners, not content duplication).

All voice below is **Thielman's own commentary** unless marked as a reported position. Thielman writes throughout as if "Paul" is the author (he defends authenticity), so "Paul" = Thielman's authorial designation, not a neutral wiki-voice claim about authorship.

---

## Claims — grouped by pericope

### 5:15–21 (Wisdom / filled in the Spirit / transition to the code)
- **[5:15–16]** Walking carefully arises (οὖν) from the preceding warning against "sons of disobedience"; believers must "watch carefully how you walk," "not as unwise [ἄσοφοι, asophoi] but as wise [σοφοί, sophoi]." "redeeming the time" = ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν (exagorazomenoi ton kairon), buying the present time out of (ἐκ) its "slavery to evil"; "the days are evil" echoes 2:2's aiōn aligned with the devil (Thielman).
- **[5:17]** διὰ τοῦτο (dia touto) refers back to "the days are evil"; understanding the Lord's will (συνίημι, syniēmi) parallels and defines "redeeming the time"; echoes Prov. 1:7 LXX (Thielman).
- **[5:18]** μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ (mē methyskesthe oinō) contrasted with πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι (plērousthe en pneumati). Thielman **rejects** specific-occasion theories (Dionysus cult — Preisker TDNT; debauched agape feast — De Wette, Gnilka; overrealized-eschatology libertinism — Barth) in favor of the view that Paul reflects a "common concern with drunkenness in the ancient literature of moral exhortation" (Isocrates, Prov. 23:31 LXX which uses the identical phrase, T. Jud. 14.1). "the positive command, and not the prohibition of drunkenness, is where Paul's emphasis lies" (following Fee).
  - On ἐν: Thielman surveys "with" (content — Best), "by" (means — Robinson, Wallace, O'Brien, Hoehner), "in" (sphere). He **adopts Heil's view**: "the preposition 'in' (ἐν) refers to being within the dynamic realm or sphere established and characterized by having been given the Spirit." Three of Heil's arguments (2007b) persuade him: πληρόω elsewhere in Eph has Christ as filler; ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία is a parallel "sphere" phrase; consistency with "in Christ" language. Present tense (per Best) carries "no special significance."
- **[5:19–20]** Five adverbial participles subordinate to πληροῦσθε. ψαλμοί/ὕμνοι/ᾠδαὶ πνευματικαί treated as "almost interchangeable" (Gnilka, Lincoln, Schnackenburg), though "spiritual" attaches special reference to spontaneous Spirit-inspired singing (Fee, cf. 1 Cor 14). εὐχαριστοῦντες shifts toward corporate prayer; thanksgiving "in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" uses OT Yahweh-blessing language for Jesus (Thielman, high Christology), yet distinguishes Jesus from Yahweh ("God, who is also Father," τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί).
- **[5:21]** ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi) is grammatically the fifth participle under πληροῦσθε (5:18) but **conceptually begins the new section**; "functions at the same time as a transition... and as a heading over the new section." In 5:24 ὑποτάσσω recurs in the indicative as a new main verb. Worship-in-houses connects corporate worship to household (Balla; Osiek & MacDonald). — Full treatment of 5:21 below.

### Household-code framing (5:21–6:9 intro material, lines 121–151)
- Household management was a Greco-Roman commonplace (Plato, Aristotle Pol., Arius Didymus, Stoic/Jewish/Neo-Pythagorean texts; Balch, Dibelius-Greeven). Three-pair pattern (husband-wife, parents-children, master-slave) parallels Col. 3:18–4:1, 1 Pet. 2:13–3:7 (Thielman reporting scholarship).
- **Apologetic-origin thesis** (reported, then qualified): Balch (1981; 1988) argued the codes — esp. in 1 Peter — are apologetic, defending the group against charges of subversion; M. Y. MacDonald (2000) and Osiek & MacDonald (2006) extend this to Ephesians (the code makes the church less visible while retaining separation). Thielman **grants historical precedent** (Josephus, Philo, Pseudo-Phocylides) but **concludes against it for Ephesians**: "The household code in Ephesians, however, is probably not part of a strategy to ease tensions between the church and society. Unlike 1 Peter (2:15; 3:1), Ephesians makes no attempt to link domestic ethics to either defending or promoting the faith among unbelievers."
- Thielman's own account of the code's function: (1) continues ethical instruction begun at 4:17; (2) uses marriage to illustrate Christ–church relationship.
- **Pseudonymity arguments reported and rejected:** some (Crouch) see the code as a post-Pauline taming of a Spirit-prompted equality impulse (Gal. 3:28); others (Dibelius-Greeven, Lincoln, MacDonald) as accommodation; Best (1997a) sees an idealism (assuming wholly-Christian households) inconsistent with the real Paul. Thielman: "none of these arguments is compelling," citing continuity with 1 Thess. 4:11 and Rom. 13:1–7.

### 5:22–24 (Wives)
- **[5:22]** No verb in the best text (𝔓46, B); ὑποτασσόμενοι must be supplied from 5:21. Wives submit to "their **own**" (ἴδιος, idios) husbands — restricts scope to marriage; "There is certainly no hint that all women should submit to all men" (Thielman, following Hoehner, Muddiman). "Paul's understanding of the equality of men and women owes more to the OT than to these [Greco-Roman] discussions."
- **[5:22]** "as to the Lord" (ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ) — Thielman interprets it via the clearer 6:7 ("as for the Lord and not for human beings"): the husband "does not have the authority of Christ, except in the case of marriage, and then only by analogy, not in reality. Christ is the submissive party's authority."
- **[5:23]** κεφαλή (kephalē) — the crux; "its precise meaning is not self-evident." — Full treatment below.
- **[5:23]** "He himself [αὐτός] is Savior of the body [σώματος]" (σωτήρ, sōtēr) — Thielman: kephalē implies authority, but Paul correlates head with savior; "his primary emphasis lies in his use of this authority to save the church." Husband's headship is "patterned after Christ's headship," which is used "not to control the church but to reconcile it... at the cost of his own life."
- **[5:24]** "in everything" (ἐν παντί, en panti) — Thielman **rejects** the "author made a mistake" reading (Best: unrealistic idealism; Muddiman: enthusiasm "spilled over") and **adopts** the qualified reading (Lincoln, O'Brien, Hoehner): not "woodenly... in everything no matter how harmful, silly, or sinful"; readers would "make exceptions in the hard cases." Parallel: Musonius Rufus on obeying parents "in all things." "The rhetorical force of ἐν παντί is focused on the importance of the wife's submission."

### 5:25–33 (Husbands + Christ/church mystery)
- **[5:25]** ἀγαπάω (agapaō): husbands love "just as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her." "the sweeping nature of the demand placed on the wife (ἐν παντί)... is therefore matched by an equally sweeping demand on the husband" — self-sacrifice of his own life. "Here Paul breaks the boundaries of traditional Greco-Roman advice on marriage" (contrast Plutarch, Pseudo-Phocylides, Musonius, Pseudo-Aristotle who counsel love/companionship but not life-expending sacrifice).
- **[5:26]** "sanctify" (ἁγιάζω, hagiazō) "by means of cleansing" (καθαρίσας, katharisas) "with the water bath in the word" (τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐν ῥήματι). Thielman **rejects the baptismal reading** (majority: Lincoln, Best, Schnackenburg, Pokorný) and **adopts the minority metaphorical reading** (O'Brien, Hoehner): λουτρόν (loutron, not βαπτίζω) is the common word for ceremonial/bridal baths; the phrase is "a metaphorical reference to the cleansing power of the gospel." ῥῆμα (rhēma) = the gospel/word of God (cf. 6:17 rhēma theou), not a baptismal formula (rejecting Chrysostom, Theodoret, Robinson).
- **[5:27]** Bridal imagery: church presented "brilliant" (ἔνδοξος, endoxos), "not having spot or wrinkle," "holy and blameless" (recalls 1:4). Background = Greco-Roman wedding toilette merged with Ezek. 16:8–14 (Christ takes God's place, church takes Israel's; but Paul reverses Ezekiel's direction of judgment into redemption). Additional Note: Thielman takes ἵνα παραστήσῃ as **present reality** (Lincoln, Schnackenburg, Best), not future (contra Ellicott, Eadie, O'Brien); distinguishes from 2 Cor. 11:2's future betrothal — and argues this difference is **not** a sign of pseudepigraphy.
- **[5:28–30]** Husbands "obligated" (ὀφείλουσιν) to love wives "as their own bodies"; "The one who loves his own wife loves himself." Grounded in one-flesh unity (Gen. 2:24) and the widespread antique notion of husband-wife organic unity. ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei, care for)/θάλπει (thalpei, cherish) = physical/emotional nurture. Believers "are parts of his body." Additional Note 5:30: the longer reading "from his flesh and from his bones" (Gen. 2:23 allusion) is text-critically rejected (absent from 𝔓46, א, A, B).
- **[5:31–32]** Gen. 2:24 quoted (ἀντὶ τούτου, anti toutou, "on account of this," altered from LXX ἕνεκεν — showing deliberate argumentative force). Thielman: the quotation refers to **both** husband-wife union **and primarily** the Christ–church union (three arguments: 5:32b explicit application; ἀντὶ τούτου pointing to 5:29c–30; πλήν at 5:33 marking 5:31–32 as digression). Radical claim: "God has instituted marriage 'because' the church is Christ's body" — the one-flesh union "was originally intended to prefigure and to illustrate the union that Christ now has with the church."
- **[5:32]** μυστήριον (mystērion) — "a truth that could be known only through God's gracious revelation." μέγα (mega) = "**especially** mysterious" (I. Marshall). On ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω: Thielman **rejects** the view (Ellicott, Lincoln, Merz, Schnackenburg, Sampley) that Paul contrasts his reading with **rival interpretations** of Gen. 2:24; instead δέ contrasts Paul's recognition that his reading is surprising with his determination to reveal it. "this mystery" points **forward** to Paul's interpretation, not back to Gen. 2:24.
- **[5:33]** πλήν (plēn, "in any case") breaks off the digression. ὑμεῖς οἱ καθ' ἕνα + ἕκαστος = "You — every single one of you." Husband loves wife "as himself" (recalling Lev. 19:18, redefined: wife is "the closest possible neighbor"). Wife "should fear her husband" — ἵνα φοβῆται (hina phobētai), an imperatival ἵνα-subjunctive carrying "a softer, more respectful nuance than the simple imperative" (Thielman): "The husband is told emphatically to love his wife, but the command to the wife has a milder tone." The softer tone recognizes that in Greco-Roman power terms "the wife had the more difficult role."

### 6:1–4 (Children and Fathers)
- **[6:1]** ὑπακούω (hypakouō, obey) — stronger/active verb than the implied ὑποτάσσω for wives; "The emphasis on the voluntary element... is missing from the command to children." Three motivations: "in the Lord" (ἐν κυρίῳ), "right" (δίκαιος, dikaios), and Scripture's command+promise. Additional Note: Thielman accepts ἐν κυρίῳ as original (𝔓46, א, A, Ψ) against Best's omission.
- **[6:1]** Obedience assumed to be qualifiable in extreme cases (cf. Col. 3:20 "in all things"; Musonius Rufus; Philo, Josephus on when to disobey parents), though "his emphasis lies on submission."
- **[6:2–3]** "Honor your father and mother... the first commandment with a promise" (ἐντολὴ πρώτη, entolē prōtē). Thielman surveys and **rejects** readings that soften πρώτη to "weightiest/pre-eminent/most important" (Dibelius-Greeven, Best, Muddiman, BDAG) and the "first of Decalogue's second table" reading (Schnackenburg). He **adopts** the majority historic view: within the Mosaic Sinai legislation it is literally "the first commandment with a promise attached specifically to it" (the second-commandment promise being general). Promise universalized: "the land" (τῆς γῆς) dropped from Exod./Deut., turning Israel-specific promise into general long life for "the one new man." On long life (6:3): follows Alford — take the simplest sense, addressed to children in a world where 39–50% died before age 10 (Saller); generally obedient children fare better (Proverbs).
- **[6:4]** Fathers "do not provoke... to anger" (παροργίζω, parorgizō, cf. 4:26) but "bring them up" (ἐκτρέφω, ektrephō) in "training" (παιδεία, paideia) and "instruction" (νουθεσία, nouthesia) "of the Lord" (κυρίου — subjective genitive, the Lord Jesus instructs through the father). νουθεσία here admonitory, not punitive. Thielman: Paul "reins in this power" of the Roman paterfamilias.

### 6:5–9 (Slaves and Masters) — see full treatment below
- **[6:5–7]** Slaves "obey" (hypakouō) "fleshly masters" (κατὰ σάρκα, kata sarka) — subtly signals a greater Master, Christ. Five descriptive phrases: "fear and trembling" (recognition of subordinate/weak position, NOT fear of physical punishment — Thielman); "in ἁπλότητι [haplotēti] of heart" (integrity/sincerity); "as to Christ"; not "eye-service" (ὀφθαλμοδουλία, ophthalmodoulia) as "people-pleasers" (ἀνθρωπάρεσκος) but "from the inner person" (ἐκ ψυχῆς) as "slaves of Christ"; "with goodwill" (μετ' εὐνοίας, met' eunoias).
- **[6:8]** God "will repay" (κομίζω, komizō) each for good done, "whether slave or free" — eschatological reward (cf. 2 Cor. 5:10), nullifying social division (cf. Gal. 3:27–28).
- **[6:9]** Masters "do the same things"; "give up" (ἀνίημι, aniēmi) "the threat of violence" (ἀπειλή, apeilē) — "not qualified in any way"; grounded in the impartial heavenly "Master" (κύριος) who shows "no favoritism."

## Eph 5:21 mutual submission — full detail (Thielman's reading)

Thielman lays out **three interpretive options** for "submitting to one another" (ἀλλήλοις, allēlois):
1. **Full mutual submission that the code then contradicts** (Muddiman, Schnackenburg): 5:21 states the author's real egalitarian view, but he lets an "inconsistently authoritarian ethic from the tradition" slip through; the mutuality "reveals where the writer's real interest lies." — **Thielman rejects this**: "The author's own approach to the traditional household code is deeply etched into his version of it (5:25–30; 6:4, 9)," so he would not carelessly leave a contradiction.
2. **"Submission" announced as topic, then illustrated asymmetrically in 5:22–6:9** (Theodoret in the 5th c., Ellicott, Robinson, O'Brien, Hoehner, Walden): ἀλλήλοις does not mean all-submit-to-all. — Thielman calls this "much more likely" and grants it "the great merit of assigning to ὑποτάσσω its normal meaning" (Spicq: "accepting the exact place God has assigned").
3. **Even those in authority "submit" (serve) their subordinates** (Jerome, Calvin — "Even kings and governors rule that they may serve"; Eadie, Bruce, Lincoln, Best, Helton): a genuine reciprocity of service, though the words ὑποτάσσω/ὑπακούω are never used of the superior party. — **Thielman judges this "best."**

Thielman's synthesis: Paul's prior uses of ἀλλήλων in Ephesians (4:2 bearing with; 4:25 members of one another; 4:32 kind to one another) are **fully reciprocal**, so the reader hears 5:21 in "a fully reciprocal sense" — "there is a sense in which everyone is involved in serving others" (supported by 1 Cor. 16:15–16). **Crucially, this reciprocity does NOT flatten the code's asymmetry:** "The submission of those mentioned in the household code is not the same type in each instance — in the code itself, husbands, fathers, and masters are never told to submit to, obey, or fear their wives, children, and slaves." The head "retains his position of authority," but "his use of that authority is tempered by an attitude of service." So 5:21 **both** introduces genuine mutuality/service **and** "prepares the ground for the distinctive approach that the household code takes to the responsibilities of husbands, fathers, and masters." It "means more than simply 'obey whom you are supposed to'" but does not equalize the roles.

On "in the fear of Christ" (φόβος, phobos): "something more than deference but less than terror" (Hoehner) — respect for Christ to whom God subjected (ὑπέταξεν) all powers, "tempered with a knowledge of the incomprehensible vastness of his love."

**Net (Thielman's position):** 5:21 is genuinely and mutually about service, but does **not** dissolve the hierarchical structure of the ensuing code — it is asymmetrical submission softened/redefined by mutual service, not egalitarian equalization. This is a mediating complementarian reading.

## Kephalē debate — full detail (5:23)

Thielman: "The term 'head' (κεφαλή, kephalē) is the critical element in the analogy, but its precise meaning is not self-evident."

**Reported lexical background:** "It was not commonly used in ancient Greek as a metaphor for an authority or leader (Perriman 1994)," though it appears with authority connotations in the LXX (Judg. 11:11; 2 Sam. 22:44) — but there always of authority over **groups**, not a single person (Perriman, Osiek).

**The "source/no-authority" reading (reported, then rejected):** "A few interpreters... have argued that there are no connotations of authority in Paul's use of it in 5:23. Κεφαλή implies that the husband is the resource for the fulfillment of the wife, just as in 4:15–16 Christ, as the head of his church-body, equips and encourages the church's growth (e.g., B. Mickelsen and A. Mickelsen 1986)." [This is the "head = source, not authority" egalitarian position.]

**Thielman's own position — kephalē DOES carry authority — two reasons:**
1. **Context signals hierarchy:** the instruction to the wife to "fear" her husband (5:33, cf. 5:21), not repeated to the husband, "reveals a hierarchical element." Decisively, the "close verbal relationship between 5:21–23 and 1:20–23": in 1:20–23 Christ's headship (κεφαλή) is defined by God's subjection (ὑποτάσσω) of all things to Christ; "This same pairing of the noun κεφαλή with the verb ὑποτάσσω in 5:21–23 indicates that here too κεφαλή carries an authoritative nuance."
2. **Cultural expectation:** readers understood κεφαλή as a metaphor for the husband's authority (Plutarch, Conj. praec. 142e: control [κρατεῖν] ought to be exercised by the man over the woman "as the soul controls the body [σώματος]"; Merz).

**But Thielman immediately qualifies the authority:** the differences from Plutarch are "important" — Plutarch's advice is pragmatic; Paul's arises from Christology. Plutarch tells the husband to "control" (κρατεῖν) the wife; "Paul never tells husbands to control their wives, only wives to submit." Paul "qualifies the husband's authority by describing his headship as patterned after Christ's headship over the church" — authority used "not to control the church but to reconcile it to God at the cost of his own life" (2:13, 16; 5:2). The parallelism head/savior (κεφαλή/σωτήρ, table at lines 239–243) shows the primary emphasis is on saving/nurturing use of authority. "Paul pictures the wife's submission as the recognition of the authority of a husband who imitates the self-sacrificial, nurturing, and supporting roles that Christ fills."

**Bedale/Grudem framing note:** The prompt asked for "Grudem vs Bedale on kephalē." **Neither Bedale nor Grudem is named in this slice.** The debate is framed here as **Perriman** (lexical skeptic re: authority metaphor) and **the Mickelsens** ("head = source/resource," the egalitarian position Thielman rejects) versus Thielman's own "authority-but-Christologically-redefined" reading. Do not attribute Bedale or Grudem to this slice.

## Marriage as mystery (5:32) — full detail

- The quotation of Gen. 2:24 (5:31) is deployed with genuine argumentative force (ἀντὶ τούτου deliberately substituted for LXX ἕνεκεν τούτου).
- Thielman: the quotation refers "probably... to both themes, but **primarily to the unity of Christ and the church**." Three arguments: (1) 5:32b's explicit application; (2) ἀντὶ τούτου points to 5:29c–30 (Christ's care for his body); (3) πλήν (5:33) marks 5:31–32 as part of the Christ-church digression.
- **Radical claim (Thielman's, attributed to Paul):** "Paul is saying in 5:31 that God has instituted marriage 'because' the church is Christ's body... the union of husband and wife in 'one flesh' was originally intended to **prefigure and to illustrate** the union that Christ now has with the church." This became knowable only after Christ's death created the multiethnic church (2:14–15; 3:8–11), hence μυστήριον (mystērion) — revealed truth (1:9; 3:3–4, 9; 6:19).
- μέγα (mega) = "especially mysterious" (quoting I. Marshall 1999: "the greatness of the degree to which the thing... is what it is").
- **ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω (egō de legō):** Thielman **rejects** the common view (Ellicott, Lincoln, Merz, Schnackenburg, Sampley) that Paul contrasts his reading against **rival interpretations** of Gen. 2:24 (he'd have specified them). Instead δέ contrasts Paul's awareness that his interpretation is "surprising" with his "determination, nevertheless, to reveal it." "This mystery" points **forward** to Paul's interpretation, not back to the Genesis text.
- Thielman does not deny the ordinary one-flesh reading of Gen. 2:24 is also true (Paul uses it in 1 Cor. 6:16 and here in the husband-love argument); Gen. 2:24 supports **both** unions, but the Christ-church reference is primary.

## Slavery (6:5–9) — how Thielman handles it

Thielman's headline framing (lines 469–471, 517, 523–527): he **explicitly resists** two readings — (a) the traditional "no approval but no disapproval" acceptance of slavery (Meyer 1880, "most commentators"), and (b) the stronger view that the passage gives **theological support** for slavery benefiting the slaveholder (Glancy 2006; Harrill 2006). Thielman: "this passage is more radical than the account of it given in either of these readings."

His argument:
- The passage assumes a "level of mutuality and reciprocity... between master and slave" that "creates an atmosphere in which it would have been difficult for slavery to survive if the advice of the passage had been rigorously followed." The fault lies not with the text but with "the failure of those who received the passage as authoritative both in antiquity and in more recent times to live out its radical implications."
- **"fleshly masters" (κατὰ σάρκα)** subtly relativizes the earthly master under Christ the true κύριος.
- **"as to Christ" (6:5) / "as for the Lord" (6:7):** Thielman **directly and repeatedly rebuts Harrill (2006):** Harrill argued (i) that the author, per ancient optical theory and slave-control ideology, wanted slaves to identify their masters with the all-seeing Lord; (ii) that slaves must cede their inner selves (ψυχαί) to masters; (iii) that masters are "the only people in the passage directly accountable to the Lord." Thielman: "the master is factored out of the equation and replaced with the Lord" — it is "almost the opposite" of Harrill's reading; Harrill's comment is "very wide of the mark" / "misconstrue[s] its meaning." He grounds the rebuttal in the undisputed Paul's stress on sincerity in one's absence (Phil. 2:12; 2 Cor. 10:11).
- **6:8:** eschatological repayment (κομίζω) "whether slave or free" — against Harrill's "mundane master-given rewards" reading; Thielman prefers eschatological reward (parallel 2 Cor. 5:10). "ultimately there is no difference between slave and free in God's eyes."
- **6:9 "do the same things":** Thielman **rejects the minimizing reading** (Westcott: "identity of spirit and not identity of action"; "most interpreters") and argues "the radical nature of the statement should not be downplayed," on three grounds: contextual movement toward mutuality; the Jesus-tradition ethic that authorities become slaves (Mark 10:41–45; John 13); the anthropology/soteriology of Eph 1–3 (unity in sin and in new creation).
- **The key move — abolishing the threat of violence:** masters must "give up" (ἀνίημι) "the threat of violence" (ἀπειλή), which Thielman (citing Bradley, Saller, W.V. Harris, Garnsey) identifies as "the primary foundation of the institution." "The command is not qualified in any way... they must give up threatening entirely. **With this command, Paul has cut the thread that held the institution of slavery together.**" Grounded in the impartial heavenly Master (no favoritism; Deut. 10:17 etc.; extended from ethnic to social impartiality, cf. Gal. 3:28).
- Summary voice: slaves retain freedom of inner attitude; masters "in a sense, [are] to submit to their slaves (5:21)"; "without the threat of violence, the whole system will theoretically collapse." "the wall between slave and free also has to crumble" (parallel to 2:14 Jew/Gentile wall).

Slice continues past 6:9 into "Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)": intro to the armor-of-God passage. Not part of my assigned scope (5:15–6:9); flagging for whichever slice owns 6:10–24. Notable content present if needed: structure (6:10–17 armor / 6:18–20 prayer, grammatically linked via δέξασθε + participles); the **pseudonymity debate** — some (Lincoln, Schnackenburg, Sellin, Beker) see 6:18–20 as an edit of Col. 4:2–4 portraying Paul as a legendary martyr; Thielman **rejects** this (following Muddiman), reading it as authentic (cf. Rom. 15:30–32; Phil. 1:19–20); and **Lincoln's peroratio/ἐπίλογος + prebattle-speech thesis** (1995), which Thielman finds "helpful in a general sense" but ultimately not a conscious construction (differences: shorter than prebattle speeches; emphasizes enemy strength not weakness, 6:12). The armor pieces (truth, righteousness, gospel-preparation, faith, salvation, word/rhēma) each recapitulate earlier letter themes.

## Named scholars / positions cited (in this slice)
- **Balch (1981; 1988):** apologetic-origin thesis for household codes (esp. 1 Peter), rooted in ancient political philosophy. Reported.
- **M. Y. MacDonald (2000); Osiek & MacDonald (2006); Merz (2000):** extend apologetic/social-strategy reading to Ephesians. Reported; Thielman qualifies/rejects for Eph.
- **Best (E. Best, 1997a; 1998):** household code betrays idealism inconsistent with real Paul; "in everything" a mistake; omits ἐν κυρίῳ (6:1); "with the Spirit" (content). Reported and largely rejected by Thielman.
- **Muddiman (2001):** 5:21 mutuality "reveals where the writer's real interest lies" (rejected); but rejects pseudonymity of 6:18–20 (Thielman agrees).
- **Heil (2007b):** ἐν πνεύματι = sphere/realm reading. **Adopted by Thielman.**
- **Fee (1994):** emphasis on the positive command; "spiritual songs" as spontaneous. Followed.
- **Perriman (1994):** kephalē rarely an authority metaphor in Greek. Reported (lexical caution).
- **B. Mickelsen & A. Mickelsen (1986):** kephalē = resource/source, no authority (egalitarian). **Reported and rejected.**
- **O'Brien (1999); Hoehner (2002):** metaphorical (non-baptismal) reading of "water bath"; qualified "in everything." Followed by Thielman.
- **Lincoln (1990; 1995):** baptismal reading of 5:26 (rejected); peroratio thesis (partly accepted); pseudonymity (rejected).
- **Schnackenburg (1991):** various; often reported.
- **Harrill (2006); Glancy (2006):** slavery passage as pro-slaveholder / slave-control ideology. **Reported and vigorously rejected by Thielman.**
- **Meyer (1880); Westcott (1906):** minimizing/neutral readings of the slavery passage. Reported, resisted.
- **I. Marshall (1999):** "great mystery" = "especially mysterious." Adopted.
- **Crouch (1972); Dibelius & Greeven (1953):** codes as taming/accommodation. Reported, rejected.
- **Alford (1857):** "simplest sense" of the long-life promise. Adopted.
- Ancient sources cited: Plutarch (Conj. praec.), Aristotle (Pol.), Plato, Musonius Rufus, Pseudo-Phocylides, Pseudo-Aristotle (Oec.), Philo, Josephus, Isocrates, T. Jud., Diodorus Siculus; text-critical witnesses 𝔓46, א, A, B, D, F, G, Ψ; social historians Saller (1994), Bradley (1987), W. V. Harris (2001), Garnsey (1996), Balla (2003).

## Notable Greek terms with glosses (as given by Thielman)
- **hypotassomenoi / hypotassō** (ὑποτασσόμενοι / ὑποτάσσω) — submitting / ordering oneself underneath; voluntary submission when passive of persons (5:21, 22, 24; used indicatively as new main verb at 5:24).
- **allēlois / allēlōn** (ἀλλήλοις) — "to one another"; in Eph consistently fully reciprocal (4:2, 25, 32).
- **plērousthe en pneumati** (πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι) — "be filled in the Spirit"; ἐν = sphere/realm (Thielman/Heil).
- **kephalē** (κεφαλή) — "head"; Thielman: carries authority nuance, but Christologically redefined toward saving/nurturing.
- **sōtēr** (σωτήρ) — "Savior" (5:23), correlated with kephalē.
- **sōma / sōmatos** (σῶμα) — "body" (church as Christ's body; wife as husband's body).
- **agapate / agapaō** (ἀγαπάω) — husbands' self-giving love (5:25, 28, 33).
- **ektrephei / thalpei** (ἐκτρέφει / θάλπει) — care for / cherish (5:29; ektrephō again 6:4).
- **loutron / tō loutrō tou hydatos** (λουτρόν) — "(water) bath"; Thielman: bridal-bath metaphor, not baptism (βαπτίζω/βάπτισμα deliberately avoided).
- **rhēma / en rhēmati** (ῥῆμα) — "word"; = the gospel/word of God (cf. 6:17), not a baptismal formula.
- **mystērion** (μυστήριον) — revealed mystery; **mega** (μέγα) = "especially" great/mysterious (5:32).
- **egō de legō** (ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω) — "but I am speaking"; δέ = surprising-but-I'll-say-it, not contrast with rival readings.
- **plēn** (πλήν) — "in any case"; breaks off the digression (5:33).
- **phobos / phobeō / hina phobētai** (φόβος / ἵνα φοβῆται) — fear/respect ("more than deference but less than terror"); wife's imperatival ἵνα-subjunctive carries a softer tone (5:33).
- **hypakouete / hypakouō** (ὑπακούω) — obey (children 6:1; slaves 6:5) — stronger/active than the implied submission of wives.
- **en kyriō** (ἐν κυρίῳ) — "in the Lord"; incorporation-into-Christ language (6:1).
- **entolē prōtē** (ἐντολὴ πρώτη) — "first commandment (with a promise)"; πρώτη = literally first in Mosaic sequence (6:2).
- **paideia / nouthesia** (παιδεία / νουθεσία) — training / instruction-admonition (6:4); nouthesia here admonitory not punitive.
- **kata sarka** (κατὰ σάρκα) — "fleshly" (masters, 6:5), relativizing earthly authority.
- **haplotēs / haplotēti** (ἁπλότης) — integrity, inner sincerity (6:5).
- **ophthalmodoulia** (ὀφθαλμοδουλία) — "eye-service" (first attested here + Col. 3:22); **anthrōpareskos** (ἀνθρωπάρεσκος) — "people-pleaser."
- **ek psychēs** (ἐκ ψυχῆς) — "from the inner person" (6:6).
- **eunoia / met' eunoias** (εὔνοια) — "with goodwill" (6:7), a virtue slaveholders prized.
- **komizō** (κομίζω) — receive/be repaid (in kind), here eschatological (6:8).
- **apeilē** (ἀπειλή) — "threat (of violence)"; **aniēmi** (ἀνίημι) — "give up," masters must abandon it entirely (6:9).
